title: Equivariant Spherical Transformer for Efficient Molecular Modeling
claim: Conventional operations process each sampled orientation independently; ours serializes orientations and uses a Transformer to model dependencies across all of them.
layout: 4 stacked panels (a–d), left-to-right flows, sphere stacks along a diagonal axis
description: The figure has four panels. The top panel (a) has two boxes. The left box, the harmonic domain, shows degree-1 and degree-2 steerable vector blocks (orange and blue cells, indexed by m). Fourier arrows (F and F^-1) lead to the right box, the spherical spatial domain. There, spherical harmonic lobes add up to a red-blue sphere f(p), which is discretized into a dotted sphere with a colorbar. Panel (b) shows a tensor product: a blue vector, a gray 3D Clebsch-Gordan cube and an orange vector, joined by × signs. Panel (c) shows conventional point-wise processing: stacked spheres along a channel axis feed arrows into a box with channel concatenation and projection formulas. Panel (d) is the proposed EST. Stacked spheres along a sample-point axis go through serialization, relative orientation embeddings, a Transformer with attention brackets, and spherization, ending in output spheres. Blue and red heat-map spheres dominate the visual.
caption: Overview of operations in the spherical spatial domain. (a) Examples of group representation. A Fourier transform is applied to project steerable vectors onto the spatial domain, which are then stored through sampling (i.e., discretization). (b) Tensor product operation. Steerable vectors are combined using the Clebsch-Gordan coefficient C. (c) Conventional orientation-wise (point-wise) operation. Features are processed independently at each sampling orientation s. A shared neural network (with linear projection W and activation σ(·)) acts only across channels (c = 1, . . . , C) within the same orientation⃗ps=i, neglecting cross-orientational relationships. (d) Proposed EST operation. A Transformer-based architecture that explicitly models dependencies across all pairs of orientations (s = 1, . . . , S), enabling the capture of complex, cross-orientational geometric correlations.
abstract: Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced the modeling of 3D molecular structure by leveraging group representations. However, message passing built only from exactly equivariant operations can have restricted practical expressiveness at a fixed representation degree. We introduce the Equivariant Spherical Transformer (EST), a plug-and-play module that applies Transformer attention to spherical spatial representations obtained from group representations. EST explicitly mixes information across sampled orientations, unlike prior orientation-wise spherical operations, while retaining a strong approximate equivariant inductive bias through near-uniform spherical sampling. As demonstrated by our experiments on challenging benchmarks like OC20, MPtrj and QM9, EST-based models achieve state-of-the-art performance. For the complex molecular systems within OC20, small models empowered by EST can outperform some larger models and those using additional data. We characterize the ideal closed-domain condition under which the continuous operation is exactly equivariant and empirically quantify the finite-sampling accuracy--equivariance--memory trade-off used in practice.
